tips.responsible.body: You’re taking someone into your life for many years, often 10–15, who will become a member of your family. So don’t decide by looks alone: check whether the dog fits your lifestyle, your home and your family. Pacsi helps with this too, with its filters, the Matchmaker quiz and the comparison tool.
tips.bred.body:
Find out what the breed you like was bred and originally used for, and think about whether you can meet its instincts. A hunting dog would sniff and run, a herding dog would herd, a guard dog would guard – even if there is no job for it at your place.

For example, the Dalmatian, star of 101 Dalmatians, was originally a coach dog that ran alongside horse-drawn carriages as an escort and guard. It still needs plenty of running, has a guarding instinct, and because of its spirited temperament it is not specifically recommended for homes with small children.

You can also look up where a breed comes from and what it was used for in the breed card descriptions.
tips.checklist.body:
• Look at the puppy’s parents and the conditions they are kept in.
  • Ask for pedigree papers (FCI/MEOESZ, the Hungarian Kennel Association) and the parents’ health screenings (e.g. hips, eyes, heart).
  • The puppy should be at least 8 weeks old, microchipped and have a vaccination record.
  • Avoid “cheap, available immediately” adverts – they often come from puppy farms.
  • Ask for a written sales contract.
tips.puppytest.h: 🐶 Puppy test: which puppy suits you?
tips.puppytest.body:
Even within a breed it matters a lot which puppy from the litter comes home with you: that is how a good dog ends up in a good home. Breeders call this a puppy test. Already at 6 weeks old it reveals a lot about a puppy’s personality, for example:

  • how much it likes people,
  • whether it is afraid of noises,
  • how easy or hard it is to motivate, and with what (food, toys, praise),
  • how independent and how quick to learn it is.
Ask the breeder whether they have done a puppy test, and which puppy they recommend for your family.
tips.adopt.body:
Plenty of purebred dogs and mixed breeds are waiting in shelters and breed rescues. What’s more, an adult dog’s character is already known.

With a rescue dog, expert help – for example from a dog trainer – is even more important. As a lay owner you can’t always see what physical traits or illnesses it has, or whether it has suffered physical or emotional trauma. Yet you have to reckon with these when socialising it after adoption. For instance, the dog may:

  • be antisocial towards other dogs, pets or people,
  • be terrified of people or other animals,
  • be hard to motivate, and so hard to train.
tips.legal.body:
• Microchip and registration.
  • Annual rabies vaccination.
  • The municipal dog census.
For information only – check the current legislation and local regulations.
tips.flat.body: The French Bulldog, the Pug or the English Bulldog are cute, but breathing, eye and spine problems are common in them. If you choose one, get it only from health-screened parents with open nostrils.
tips.cost.h: 💶 What to expect in the first year
tips.cost.body:
• Food (depending on size, this is the biggest item)
  • Vaccinations, worming, parasite protection
  • Dog school, equipment, bed
  • Groomer for breeds that need a lot of grooming
  • A reserve for unexpected vet costs, or insurance
The €–€€€ rating on breed cards shows the relative monthly running costs.
tips.newsletter.body: Every Thursday: the breed of the week, owner tips and a little brain-teaser – free, unsubscribe any time.
tips.about.p1: The traits describe the average for each breed; individual dogs may differ. The portraits are original illustrations made with artificial intelligence. “Pacsi” is Hungarian for “high five”.
tips.about.p2: Privacy: no sign-up, and we don’t collect personal data; favourites are stored only on this device. {host} keeps anonymous, cookie-free visitor statistics on its own server (e.g. which breeds and filters are most popular) – you can switch this off above, in Settings.
